title: Aurora Labs x Redwood — Guided onboarding / first production launch checklist interview
summary: Aurora Labs shared onboarding friction integrating LLM inference APIs into their product: key management confusion (test vs prod), first request reliability (timeouts/retries), streaming disconnect handling, and uncertainty about what “production-ready” means. They want an in-product checklist that is progressive (first response → streaming → observability → rate limits → rollout/rollback), with a mix of automatic validation (first successful request, first streaming session, dashboard visit) and explicit “attest” items (timeouts set, retries implemented, PII policy reviewed). Aurora stressed that validation should be per project/environment (not just per org), and that any telemetry must avoid customer prompt content and be transparent. Redwood walked through initial concepts for Console checklist + telemetry signals, and captured expectations for a minimal “first production launch” definition (monitoring + usage/cost visibility, sensible client-side retries/timeouts, quota handling, and a rollback/fallback plan).
topics: Onboarding funnel friction: API key creation, environment separation, and first request
Streaming: disconnects, SSE behavior, and retry semantics
What counts as “production”: minimal safeguards and rollout/rollback expectations
Checklist validation: automatic vs manual/attestation steps
Telemetry/privacy constraints: no prompt content, retention expectations, and transparency
questions: Should checklist completion be tracked per project, per environment (test/prod), or both?
What’s an acceptable validation delay for “first successful request” (seconds vs minutes)?
Which items must be auto-validated vs allowed as self-attestation to avoid false negatives?
How should Redwood communicate telemetry collection and redaction to developers in-product?
What is Aurora’s minimum bar for calling an integration “production launched”?
action_items: Redwood (Elliot Price) — Share draft doc outline for “First production launch” page + checklist mapping; due 2026-02-03
Redwood (Dylan Brooks) — Follow up with proposed validation signals (first success, first streaming, dashboard visit) + expected lag/edge cases; due 2026-02-04
Redwood (Nikhil Sharma) — Send 2–3 candidate checklist step lists (short vs long) for Aurora feedback; due 2026-02-05
Aurora (Ravi Desai) — Provide a redacted snippet of current retry/timeout + streaming handling (what they do today); due 2026-02-06
Aurora (Elena Petrova) — Confirm internal requirements for telemetry retention/data residency and what they consider “no content”; due 2026-02-06
next_steps: Redwood to circulate checklist draft and validation approach for async comments.
Schedule 30-min follow-up to review revised step ordering and copy (incl. rate limit/quota step).
Aurora to share 2–3 onboarding “gotchas” from recent incidents/tickets to ensure checklist prevents repeats.
transcript:
Meeting: Aurora Labs x Redwood — Guided onboarding / first production launch checklist interview
Date: 2026-01-28
Start time: 09:00 PT
Duration: 48 min
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood), Nikhil Sharma (Redwood), Dylan Brooks (Redwood), Elliot Price (Redwood), Maya Chen (Aurora), Ravi Desai (Aurora), Elena Petrova (Aurora)

Auto-summary (Fireflies):
- Aurora wants clearer path from signup to production, especially around keys, retries/timeouts, and observability.
- Redwood exploring in-console checklist with validation signals; Aurora cautions about false positives/negatives.


[00:00] Alex Martinez: Cool. Thanks everyone for making time. Um, this is basically, like, user research slash technical deep dive. We’re building a guided onboarding in the Console for the hosted API, and we’re talking to a handful of teams about where you got stuck and what “production ready” actually means.

[00:18] Maya Chen: Yep, makes sense.

[00:20] Alex Martinez: Quick intros? I’m Alex, I run DevEx at Redwood.

[00:24] Nikhil Sharma: Nikhil, PM on hosted API onboarding.

[00:27] Dylan Brooks: Dylan, eng lead on Console and some of the tooling.

[00:30] Elliot Price: Elliot, docs.

[00:32] Maya Chen: Maya, platform engineering manager at Aurora. We’re the team that integrates all these APIs and then supports product teams.

[00:40] Ravi Desai: Ravi, staff engineer. I wrote most of our first integration, and I’m on call for it, so, yeah.

[00:46] Elena Petrova: Elena, security. I’m mostly here to make sure we don’t do anything… exciting with data.

[00:52] Alex Martinez: Great. So, first topic: when you tried Redwood, what was the first friction point? Like literally, signup to first successful response.

[01:02] Ravi Desai: Honestly? API keys. It wasn’t “hard” but it was easy to do the wrong thing. We generated a key, put it in our CI, then later realized we were using what you call a… test key? Or like a dev environment key. And then we got 401s when we tried to run from production VPC.

[01:23] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah, that’s a super common one. Like wrong org/project, wrong key, wrong environment.

[01:28] Ravi Desai: Exactly. And the error message said unauthorized, but it wasn’t clear if it was “key invalid” or “key valid but not allowed.”

[01:36] Dylan Brooks: That’s helpful. So, key creation flow and error taxonomy.

[01:40] Maya Chen: Also, the first request path. The docs have a quickstart, but we needed to do it in TypeScript and we wanted streaming. The streaming example we found didn’t exactly match the SDK version we installed.

[01:55] Elliot Price: Was it the README snippet or the docs page?

[01:59] Maya Chen: It was a docs page, I think, but it linked to a GitHub snippet. Could be our fault. But we had to tweak it.

[02:07] Elliot Price: Got it. We’re trying to make those canonical and consistent across languages.

[02:12] Alex Martinez: When you say “first request path” — like literally the request didn’t work, or it worked but it was fragile?

[02:19] Ravi Desai: First it worked. Then it didn’t. Like, timeouts. We had default fetch timeout, which is basically none, and then the request hung and our worker got stuck. So we added timeouts. Then we realized we need retries, but retries + streaming is weird.

[02:38] Maya Chen: Yeah and we didn’t know what your recommended retry policy is. Like 429 vs 500 vs disconnect mid stream.

[02:47] Nikhil Sharma: That’s exactly one of the checklist items we’re debating: do we make “add retries/timeouts” a required step before “production.”

[02:55] Elena Petrova: For production, yes. For “hello world”, no.

[02:58] Alex Martinez: Makes sense. So if we had an in-product checklist, what would the first few steps be?

[03:06] Maya Chen: Step one: create API key. But it has to tell you what key you created. Like “test key” vs “prod key”, and what it can access.

[03:16] Ravi Desai: And make it obvious where to put it. Environment variables, not paste it into code.

[03:21] Alex Martinez: Okay.

[03:23] Maya Chen: Step two: install SDK and run a first request. Preferably copy paste. But it needs to work.

[03:31] Ravi Desai: Ideally it auto-detects that we did it? Like, I don’t want to come back and click “I did it.”

[03:39] Dylan Brooks: Right, validation signals. We can detect first successful request at the gateway level. But there’s nuance: we have to attribute it to the right project, and there’s some delay.

[03:50] Ravi Desai: Delay is fine if it’s like a minute. Not if it’s a day.

[03:54] Dylan Brooks: It’s not a day. More like seconds to a couple minutes depending on aggregation.

[03:59] Maya Chen: Per project is key. We have multiple internal services. One might be integrated and another not.

[04:07] Nikhil Sharma: So checklist should be per project, not per org.

[04:10] Maya Chen: Yep.

[04:12] Alex Martinez: What about streaming? You mentioned streaming disconnects.

[04:16] Ravi Desai: Yeah. We used SSE. We’d get partial tokens then it would just stop. No final message. And we weren’t sure if it was our network, or Redwood closing idle, or what.

[04:29] Dylan Brooks: Do you remember if you were behind a proxy, like Cloudflare, or internal gateway?

[04:33] Ravi Desai: We have an internal gateway, yes. And we saw some buffering, I think.

[04:38] Maya Chen: Also, the example we used didn’t set keep-alive. Not sure if that matters.

[04:43] Dylan Brooks: It can. Also, some clients don’t flush. We’ve seen that.

[04:48] Alex Martinez: If the checklist had a streaming step, what would “done” mean? Like, first streaming response happened?

[04:56] Ravi Desai: Yeah, but define it. Like “we saw at least one stream event and then a completed event.”

[05:03] Dylan Brooks: Right, we can define “stream session” as receiving first chunk and then terminal event, or something. But it’s tricky because disconnects happen and we don’t want to block you forever.

[05:15] Maya Chen: Maybe it can be “you successfully started a stream” and then separately “you handled disconnects.”

[05:21] Nikhil Sharma: Handling disconnects is hard to validate.

[05:24] Maya Chen: Exactly. That should be an “attestation” step. Like check the box and link to docs.

[05:31] Alex Martinez: That’s helpful framing: auto-validate where it’s unambiguous, and allow self-attest where it’s more of a practice.

[05:40] Elena Petrova: But attestation is fine if the consequences are clear. Like “If you skip timeouts your workers will hang.”

[05:47] Elliot Price: Copy that. We can write it that way.

[05:51] Alex Martinez: Let’s talk about “production.” When you say “we launched to production”, what did you have to do internally?

[05:58] Maya Chen: We need observability. Latency, error rate, and cost. If we can’t see token usage per service, we can’t operate it.

[06:09] Ravi Desai: And rate limits. We hit 429s during a test because we ran a backfill job, and then we didn’t understand if it was per key, per org, per IP.

[06:21] Nikhil Sharma: It’s per project and per org, and depends on your plan. But yeah, it’s not obvious.

[06:28] Ravi Desai: Right. The checklist should tell you “here’s how 429 works, and here’s what to do.” Like exponential backoff with jitter, respect retry-after, etc.

[06:39] Dylan Brooks: And maybe link to quotas settings in Console.

[06:42] Maya Chen: Yes. And also, I want to set a limit. Like, I want to say “don’t let this exceed $X per day.”

[06:50] Nikhil Sharma: We have spend controls on the roadmap. Today, you can set some quota caps. We can link to what’s available.

[06:58] Alex Martinez: For “first production launch,” would you accept a minimal checklist, like 6–8 items, vs a huge list?

[07:06] Maya Chen: Minimal. But it has to include the high-risk stuff.

[07:10] Ravi Desai: High-risk is: retries/timeouts, rate limits, monitoring, and rollback.

[07:17] Alex Martinez: Rollback meaning…?

[07:20] Ravi Desai: Like, if model output quality is bad or latency spikes, we need to switch off the feature or fall back to a smaller model or just disable. We did that with feature flags.

[07:32] Dylan Brooks: So a checklist item could be “add a kill switch / fallback.”

[07:36] Maya Chen: Yeah, and document how to do that with your API. Like, can we pin a model version? Can we change it without redeploy?

[07:45] Nikhil Sharma: You can pin model versions and you can also use routing policies, but for hosted it’s mostly via config.

[07:52] Ravi Desai: That’s another confusion: model naming. We used “llama 3.1 something” and then there was “-instruct” and “-turbo” and we weren’t sure what changed.

[08:05] Elliot Price: That’s fair. We’re trying to have stable URLs and stable model identifiers, but the ecosystem moves.

[08:12] Alex Martinez: If the checklist linked to docs, would you prefer the docs to be versioned? Like “this matches SDK vX”.

[08:18] Ravi Desai: Yes.

[08:20] Maya Chen: At least for code snippets.

[08:22] Elliot Price: Noted.

[08:24] Alex Martinez: Validation expectations: which steps should be “magically” marked complete? You already said first request. Anything else?

[08:33] Maya Chen: First dashboard visit. Like, we went to usage analytics. That could be a step.

[08:39] Ravi Desai: Also creating a production key. Like, if you make “prod key” a thing, then check that we created one.

[08:46] Dylan Brooks: That’s doable. We can detect creation events.

[08:49] Elena Petrova: Careful: “prod key” is a label, right? It doesn’t prove you’re actually using it in prod.

[08:55] Dylan Brooks: True. It’s more of a gating action.

[08:58] Alex Martinez: That’s good nuance. We don’t want false confidence.

[09:02] Nikhil Sharma: There’s also “first successful streaming session.” We can detect a stream handshake and some events.

[09:10] Ravi Desai: But be careful. We had streams that started but ended early. That shouldn’t count as “done.”

[09:16] Dylan Brooks: Right, we’d likely define it as “stream completed normally at least once.”

[09:21] Maya Chen: Or “started streaming” is enough for onboarding. The reliability stuff goes in production checklist.

[09:28] Alex Martinez: That’s a good split: onboarding vs production.

[09:31] Elliot Price: We’ve been thinking of two sections: “Get started” and “First production launch.”

[09:37] Maya Chen: Yes.

[09:39] Alex Martinez: Elena, from security side, any hard requirements for what we can collect for telemetry? Because we want to measure dropoff.

[09:48] Elena Petrova: No prompt content. Like, no user data. If you’re collecting “first request occurred,” that’s fine. But do not log the prompt. Also be explicit. If the Console is emitting events, we want to know what.

[10:04] Dylan Brooks: We’re aligned. Our plan is strict allowlist: event name + coarse properties like project_id, org_id, step_id, timestamp. No raw prompts.

[10:14] Elena Petrova: And retention. How long is this stored?

[10:17] Dylan Brooks: For onboarding funnel, we were thinking 90 days at full fidelity, then aggregated.

[10:23] Elena Petrova: Fine, as long as it’s not tied to end-user identifiers.

[10:28] Alex Martinez: It wouldn’t be. It’s org/project level.

[10:31] Maya Chen: One more thing: the checklist should not spam. Like, don’t pop a modal every time.

[10:37] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah we’re leaning to a sidebar card in Console.

[10:41] Maya Chen: Great.

[10:43] Alex Martinez: On validation lag: if you make a request, and it’s successful, you expect the checklist to tick off within… what?

[10:50] Ravi Desai: Within a minute would feel “real.” Within five minutes is okay. If it’s longer, I’ll assume it’s broken.

[10:57] Dylan Brooks: Okay, we can aim for near-real-time, but we need to handle idempotency and duplicates.

[11:04] Ravi Desai: Another thing: multi-region. We ran tests from EU.

[11:09] Dylan Brooks: We can capture region as a property, but again, privacy safe.

[11:14] Maya Chen: And the step should say “we saw a successful request” not “we saw YOUR request content.” Like reassure.

[11:22] Elliot Price: That’s a copy note for sure.

[11:26] Alex Martinez: Let’s drill on what your ideal “first production launch” checklist would be. If you had to pick, say, 7 items.

[11:34] Maya Chen: 1) Production key created and stored securely. 2) Timeouts set. 3) Retries set for 429/5xx with backoff. 4) Streaming disconnect handling if using streaming. 5) Observability: metrics and logs. 6) Rate limit/quota understanding and caps. 7) Rollback/kill switch.

[11:58] Ravi Desai: Plus: choose model and pin version. That might be part of it.

[12:04] Nikhil Sharma: Would that be mandatory?

[12:06] Ravi Desai: If model changes under you, that’s scary. So yes, pin. Even if you have a “latest” alias, at least for prod we pin.

[12:15] Maya Chen: Or have a canary. But that might be too much for “first”.

[12:20] Alex Martinez: We’re trying not to make it too heavy.

[12:23] Maya Chen: Right.

[12:25] Elliot Price: We can phrase it as “Pin a model version OR set a rollout policy.”

[12:31] Dylan Brooks: And validation could be “you selected a pinned version in config.”

[12:35] Ravi Desai: That’s good.

[12:37] Alex Martinez: What about structured output or tool calling? Do you think it belongs in onboarding steps?

[12:44] Ravi Desai: It’s nice but not required. We used structured output, but it’s advanced.

[12:50] Maya Chen: Maybe it’s optional. Like “next steps.”

[12:53] Nikhil Sharma: That’s what we were thinking: a core path and then optional enhancements.

[12:59] Alex Martinez: Great. How should we handle the “attestation” UX? Like, checkboxes? Or “mark done.”

[13:07] Maya Chen: Checkboxes with “why it matters” and a link.

[13:11] Ravi Desai: And make it easy to skip, but show “you’re skipping a risk.”

[13:17] Elliot Price: We can add small warning copy.

[13:21] Elena Petrova: Don’t force it unless it’s truly required. People will click through.

[13:26] Alex Martinez: Fair.

[13:28] Dylan Brooks: On the backend side, we were considering storing checklist state server-side so it’s consistent across sessions.

[13:35] Maya Chen: Yes. We had multiple engineers. If one completes first request, the other should see it.

[13:41] Ravi Desai: Absolutely.

[13:43] Alex Martinez: What about per-environment? Like test vs prod.

[13:48] Maya Chen: That’s tricky. We’d want separate checklists, but at least for phase one, per project is okay.

[13:55] Ravi Desai: If you can, track “prod key created” as a separate step. That’s a proxy.

[14:01] Nikhil Sharma: Makes sense.

[14:03] Alex Martinez: Let’s talk about support issues you hit. Any specific errors?

[14:09] Ravi Desai: 401s like I said. And 429s. And streaming just stopping. Also CORS when we tried from browser for a demo.

[14:19] Dylan Brooks: Hosted API from browser will hit CORS unless you proxy.

[14:23] Ravi Desai: Right, we figured that out, but we wasted time.

[14:27] Elliot Price: We should add that to troubleshooting.

[14:30] Maya Chen: Yeah, a troubleshooting link in the checklist would be good.

[14:34] Alex Martinez: Great point: a persistent “Common failures” entry.

[14:38] Nikhil Sharma: We’re hearing that across calls.

[14:41] Dylan Brooks: Also request IDs. Do you use them?

[14:44] Ravi Desai: We started to. But we didn’t know we could pass our own.

[14:48] Dylan Brooks: We support request IDs for tracing; we can add it to code samples.

[14:53] Maya Chen: That helps with support escalation.

[14:56] Alex Martinez: On the checklist validation side, would you want a step like “add request IDs”?

[15:02] Maya Chen: Maybe in production checklist as recommended.

[15:05] Ravi Desai: Yeah optional.

[15:08] Alex Martinez: Switching gears: If we add UTM parameters to docs links from Console so we can see what links are effective — any concerns?

[15:17] Elena Petrova: UTMs are fine. Just don’t include org name or anything in the URL.

[15:22] Elliot Price: It’d be generic like step_id.

[15:25] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[15:27] Maya Chen: The key is: the docs should open in new tab and then you can come back and it remembers.

[15:33] Dylan Brooks: Yep.

[15:35] Alex Martinez: Let’s dig deeper on what “first success” means. Is it any 200 response? Or also like “you got a non-empty completion.”

[15:44] Ravi Desai: Any 200 with tokens back. If it’s a 200 and empty, that’s weird.

[15:50] Dylan Brooks: We can define as “non-zero output tokens.” But we have to be careful with some endpoints.

[15:56] Nikhil Sharma: For embeddings it’s different.

[15:58] Maya Chen: For our use case it’s chat/completions.

[16:02] Alex Martinez: For phase one, we can focus on chat/generate.

[16:06] Ravi Desai: Another thought: “first repeated usage.” Like first request is easy, but we want to know if we came back.

[16:14] Nikhil Sharma: That’s more of a metric than a checklist step, but we will measure it.

[16:20] Alex Martinez: Right. We’re instrumenting completion funnel.

[16:23] Maya Chen: As long as it doesn’t impact latency.

[16:26] Dylan Brooks: It won’t; it’s async.

[16:29] Elena Petrova: Also please don’t send telemetry from SDKs without disclosure.

[16:34] Alex Martinez: Noted. Our plan is Console + backend, not auto-SDK telemetry.

[16:40] Ravi Desai: Good.

[16:42] Alex Martinez: If we sent you a draft step list, would you be willing to comment on ordering and wording?

[16:47] Maya Chen: Yes.

[16:48] Ravi Desai: Yep.

[16:50] Alex Martinez: Awesome.

[16:52] Elliot Price: One quick docs question: when you were onboarding, did you start from “Quickstart” or from API reference?

[16:58] Ravi Desai: Quickstart.

[16:59] Maya Chen: And then API reference when something didn’t match.

[17:03] Elliot Price: Did you find the reference clear?

[17:06] Ravi Desai: Mostly. The error codes could be better. Like what triggers 429, what’s retriable.

[17:12] Elliot Price: Understood.

[17:14] Nikhil Sharma: That overlaps with checklist step “handle rate limits.”

[17:18] Alex Martinez: Circling back on production: would you want the checklist to explicitly define “production launch” in Redwood’s terms? Like, “we recommend you do these to be production-ready.”

[17:29] Maya Chen: Yes, because today it’s ambiguous. Different teams have different standards.

[17:35] Ravi Desai: But be careful not to imply you guarantee reliability if we check boxes.

[17:40] Alex Martinez: Right, it’s guidance, not a certification.

[17:44] Elena Petrova: And make it clear which steps are required for compliance vs recommended. We have regulated customers.

[17:51] Nikhil Sharma: For hosted API, compliance varies, but we can keep it generic.

[17:58] Dylan Brooks: We can add “security basics” as part of production: rotate keys, least privilege, etc.

[18:04] Elena Petrova: Key rotation should be there, but again, hard to validate.

[18:09] Dylan Brooks: Attestation.

[18:10] Maya Chen: That works.

[18:12] Alex Martinez: Okay. Last area: what would make you love this onboarding checklist? Like, the “wow” moment.

[18:20] Ravi Desai: If it actually saves time. Like we don’t have to open 10 tabs. If the Console tells you what to do next and confirms you did it, that’s huge.

[18:30] Maya Chen: And if it prevents the common mistakes: wrong key, wrong endpoint, misunderstanding quotas.

[18:37] Elena Petrova: And it doesn’t collect data it shouldn’t.

[18:41] Alex Martinez: Great. We’re aligned.

[18:44] Nikhil Sharma: Can I ask one more: would you want the checklist to be dismissible?

[18:49] Maya Chen: Yes, but it should be easy to bring back.

[18:52] Ravi Desai: And maybe it auto-shows for new projects.

[18:56] Dylan Brooks: That’s doable.

[18:58] Alex Martinez: Cool. We’ll wrap soon. Let me recap what I heard.

[19:03] Alex Martinez: You want a minimal, progressive checklist with strong early steps: key creation (test vs prod clarity), first request validated automatically, streaming validated at least once, docs/snippet parity, plus a “first production launch” section with timeouts, retries, 429 guidance, observability, quotas, and rollback/kill switch. Validation should be per project; lag should be under ~5 minutes; and telemetry must be privacy-safe with no prompt content and transparent retention.

[19:35] Maya Chen: Yep.

[19:36] Ravi Desai: That’s right.

[19:38] Elena Petrova: Yes.

[19:40] Alex Martinez: Next steps: we’ll send a draft checklist and a draft “first production launch” doc outline for comments. Ravi, if you can share a redacted snippet of how you do retries/timeouts and streaming handling today, that’ll help us not write fantasy code.

[19:55] Ravi Desai: Sure, I can do that.

[19:57] Alex Martinez: Elena, if you can confirm your retention expectations and any hard “no’s” beyond prompt content, we’ll fold that into our privacy review.

[20:07] Elena Petrova: Will do.

[20:09] Alex Martinez: Awesome. Thanks all.

[20:12] Maya Chen: Thanks.

[20:13] Ravi Desai: Thank you.

[20:14] Elliot Price: Thanks everyone.

[20:16] Dylan Brooks: Appreciate it.

(Transcript continues with light small talk and scheduling; recording ended)
notes: Call was used as guided onboarding discovery input (prospect feedback). Key themes: environment/key confusion, streaming robustness, and strong preference for per-project checklist state + fast validation. Security reiterated “no prompt content” and desire for explicit telemetry transparency.
